title: Namibia's Etosha Pan Seen From Space by Sentinel-2
summary: A Copernicus Sentinel-2 image from 5 April 2026 shows Etosha National Park in northern Namibia, including its huge salt flat, in false colour. The picture shows how infrared light can reveal vegetation, water and salt across a harsh landscape.

sections.heading: A Vast Salt Flat
sections.body: The image shows Etosha National Park in northern Namibia, a game reserve built around the Etosha Pan, a large salt flat. The pan stretches roughly 130 km from east to west and covers 4760 sq km. Although it looks bright white to human eyes, the false-colour image shows its salt expanses in white, with light blue where the water holds cloudy sediment and dark blue where the water is clearer.

sections.heading: Water at Dry Season's Start
sections.body: The picture was taken at the start of the dry season, when average daily temperatures typically range from 14°C to 30°C. Water is still present in the smaller salt pans northwest of the Etosha Pan, the biggest of which is the Natukanaoka Pan, and these small lakes appear in shades of green and blue. Near the centre, the Ekuma river flows south from Lake Oponono, at about 1200 m above sea level, down to the salt flat at 1030 m. Lake Oponono can hold water from one wet season to the next and is a habitat for flamingos and cattle.

sections.heading: Red Shows Living Vegetation
sections.body: Plants appear red because healthy vegetation reflects more near-infrared light, which the satellite can detect. Around the pan, the plants are mainly grassland, savannas and mopane woodland. Mopane trees dominate the eastern and central park, show up as dark, vibrant red, and shelter elephants, giraffe and leopards. The savannahs in the west and south are home to wildebeest, lions and springbok, and even the salty pan has red patches where blue-green algae and salt-tolerant grasses have adapted.

sections.heading: How Sentinel-2 Sees Colour
sections.body: Sentinel-2 carries a multispectral imager that detects light in 13 spectral bands. The human eye sees only three: red, blue and green. This lets the mission capture near-infrared and short-wave infrared light, producing false-colour images that highlight specific features of the landscape.
